paragraphs.heading: A path of random steps
paragraphs.text: A random walk is a process that traces out a path made of one random step after another in some mathematical space. The plainest example lives on the integer number line ℤ. It starts at 0, and at each step it moves +1 or −1 with equal chance. Some texts call it a drunkard's walk.

paragraphs.heading: Why it shows up everywhere
paragraphs.text: The same picture fits a molecule wandering through a liquid or a gas, an animal searching for food, a stock price that moves up and down, and a gambler's money. Random walks are used in engineering and in many sciences, from ecology and psychology to physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, economics and sociology. Karl Pearson coined the term random walk in 1905. Sample paths can be produced by Monte Carlo simulation.

paragraphs.heading: A coin and a number line
paragraphs.text: Put a marker on zero and flip a fair coin. Heads moves it one unit right; tails moves it one unit left. After five flips the marker sits on -5, -3, -1, 1, 3 or 5. Three heads and two tails, in any order, leave it on 1, and there are 10 such orders. There are 5 ways to reach 3, and just 1 way to reach 5.

paragraphs.heading: Walks on a grid
paragraphs.text: A common model is a walk on a regular lattice, where each step jumps to another site according to some probability distribution. In a simple random walk, the marker may only hop to neighbouring sites. If it is also symmetric, each immediate neighbour is equally likely. The best-studied case is the d-dimensional integer lattice ℤᵈ.

paragraphs.heading: It keeps coming back
paragraphs.text: Let a simple random walk on ℤ run forever and it will cross every point infinitely many times. This fact goes by several names: the level-crossing phenomenon, recurrence, or gambler's ruin. The last name has a story. A gambler with limited money playing a fair game against a bank with unlimited money will eventually lose, because their money follows a random walk that hits zero at some point.

paragraphs.heading: Hitting a target
paragraphs.text: Start a one-dimensional simple random walk at 0, and pick positive integers a and b. On average it takes ab steps to first reach either b or −a. The chance that it reaches b before −a is a/(a + b). That second answer follows from the fact that a simple random walk is a martingale.

paragraphs.heading: Pascal's triangle and the normal curve
paragraphs.text: Some of these results come from Pascal's triangle. With steps of +1 or −1, there are 2ⁿ different walks of n steps, and in the simple random walk each one is equally likely. The central limit theorem says that as n grows, the chances of ending at each position approach a normal distribution.
